entities.name: Conchobar Maenmaige Ua Conchobair
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Conchobar Maenmaige Ua Conchobair (died 1189) reigned as King of Connacht from 1183 until his assassination, a turbulent period in medieval Ireland fundamentally reshaped by the nascent Anglo-Norman invasion. As the son of Ruaidrí Ua Conchobair, the last High King of Ireland, Conchobar inherited a kingdom fractured by internal dynastic rivalries and external pressures from the expanding English presence under figures like John de Courcy. His brief rule represents a critical juncture where Gaelic Irish sovereignty in the west was increasingly contested, marking a transition from traditional Irish kingship towards a landscape dominated by Anglo-Norman feudalism.

His ascent to power in 1183 was preceded by significant conflict with his own father, Ruaidrí, whom he deposed and briefly imprisoned, reflecting the intense internecine struggles characteristic of the Uí Conchobair dynasty. Conchobar Maenmaige then faced a relentless challenge from his younger brother, Cathal Crobderg Ua Conchobair, for control of Connacht, a rivalry that often involved strategic alliances with various Anglo-Norman lords. He engaged in military campaigns to assert his authority against both his Gaelic rivals and the Anglo-Normans, notably attempting to secure his borders against incursions from Ulster and Meath, though often with limited long-term success against the better-organized Norman forces.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Conchobar Maenmaige Ua Conchobair's tumultuous reign and assassination in 1189 profoundly destabilized Connacht, directly contributing to the prolonged civil war that weakened Gaelic resistance and allowed greater Anglo-Norman penetration into western Ireland.
